[MUJAHID:v2p693#2/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan defines the human as impatient in hardship and withholding in prosperity, saying this is how humanity was created.
[FARRA:v3p185/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Haluʿ means irritable and impatient; the next verses define it as despairing in harm and withholding in good, from the root pattern of jazaʿ.
[MAJAZ:v2p270/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Halāʿ is the verbal noun for the worst kind of impatience shown by one who despairs at harm and withholds good.
[TUSTARI:70:20-21/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | When a person becomes poor he grieves, and when he becomes wealthy he withholds.
[TAB-FULL:v23p266/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The human described is the disbeliever, created with intense anxiety: extreme panic combined with greed, impatience, and frustration.
[TAB-FULL:v23p266/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the person as the one who panics when harmed and withholds when given good, and says this describes associators.
[TAB-FULL:v23p266/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the disbeliever is stingy and withholds good, panicking when misfortune strikes.
[NAHHAS:v5p31/r1] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Jazūʿan and manūʿan are adjectives of halūʿ, or the meaning is that the person becomes so when touched by harm or good.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p94/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · عطية | reports | When touched by good, a person does not give thanks; when touched by harm, he does not endure it patiently.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p94/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · يحيى بن سلام | reports | When wealthy, a person withholds God's due; when poor, he asks persistently.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p226/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Harm means hardship and poverty, and one who panics does not endure patiently or seek reward.
[JISHUMI:v10p7081/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو مسلم | reports | Jazūʿan and manūʿan are accusative by proximity to halūʿan, rather than in the same grammatical role as it.
[JISHUMI:v10p7081/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Jazaʿ is the opposite of patience.
[JISHUMI:v10p7082/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · عطية عن ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains haluʿ by the following traits: when afflicted by harm, one is anxious, and when given good, one withholds it.
[JISHUMI:v10p7082/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو عبيدة وثعلب | reports | They say the person fails to give thanks when blessed and fails to be patient when afflicted.
[JISHUMI:v10p7082/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · سهل | reports | Sahl explains the traits as anxiety when poor and stinginess when prosperous.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p223#2/r10] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عباس | reports | Atiyya reports Ibn Abbas’s explanation from the following clauses: poverty makes a person impatient, while wealth makes him withhold it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p367/r17] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | هلع is anxious agitation that overtakes a person amid fears and desires; the author begins to compare it with a Prophetic saying.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p363#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | When afflicted by hardship, meaning poverty, a person despairs and neither endures nor seeks reward from God.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p113#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Some take 'the human being' as the unbeliever; others take it generally, since the verse then exempts those who pray.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p113#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Haluʿ is intense acquisitiveness and little patience; al-Farrāʾ and al-Mubarrad gloss it as fretful, while Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā says the verse itself explains it: extreme distress under harm and withholding under benefit.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p113#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · القاضي | reports | The Qāḍī argues that 'the human was created anxious' does not mean God made him inevitably blameworthy: God does not blame His own act, and believers can struggle against this trait.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p113#3/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Haluʿ has an inward psychological state and outward acts showing that state; the involuntary inner state is created by God, while speech and actions expressing it remain choices people can refrain from.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p114/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The harm and good may mean poverty and wealth, or illness and health: in hardship a person complains, and in ease withholds what is good.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p114/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The fault is not seeking relief itself but restricting concern to immediate bodily conditions; one should accept poverty or illness as God's decree and use health or wealth to seek the afterlife.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:70:18-21/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | When harmed, a person is greatly distressed; when prosperous, he withholds intensely. These three qualities are innate dispositions, actual or expected; each إذا governs its following description.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p279#10/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | “The human” denotes the species, allowing worshippers to be excepted; Ibn ʿAbbās explains halūʿ by the next two verses as quickly distressed at harm and withholding at good.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p279#10/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Halūʿ is quick distress when touched by harm and quick withholding when touched by good; one who receives good hoards it and denies it to others.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p279#10/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · محمد بن عبد الله بن طاهر | reports | When asked by Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir, Thaʿlab replied that God's own explanation is clearest.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p279#10/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | This is human temperament, but people are commanded to oppose their temperament and follow revealed law; harm may be poverty or illness and good may be wealth or health.
[QASHANI:70:17-21/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The ego is inherently a source of evil and impurity; attachment to its dark nature produces cowardice and greed, shown by despair under harm and withholding good.
[QASHANI:70:17-21/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام | reports | A prophetic saying calls consuming greed and ruinous cowardice a man’s worst traits.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p274/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ثعلب | reports | Asked by Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Tahir what hala' means, he says the following verses define it: distress makes a person intensely anxious and prosperity makes him withhold.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p275/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Human anxiety and withholding are so entrenched that humanity is described as created bearing them, as in 21:37; al-khayr here means wealth. | mentions 21:37
[SAMIN-DURR:70:20-21/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | ‘Jazu‘an’ and ‘manu‘an’ can be overlapping circumstantial states of the pronoun in ‘halu‘an’; the two time phrases modify those states.
[SAMIN-DURR:70:20-21/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Abu al-Baqa’s wording calls ‘jazu‘an’ another circumstantial but can mislead readers into treating it as separate; his stated governor shows the intended overlapping relation.
[SAMIN-DURR:70:20-21/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · مكي | reports | Makki analyzes both adjectives as predicates of an omitted ‘kana’ or ‘sara’: when harm touches him he becomes distressed, and when good touches him he becomes withholding.
[SAMIN-DURR:70:20-21/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · مكي | reports | Makki also allows the two words to modify ‘halu‘an’, but finds this distant because the time phrase must be understood before its adjective; the author rejects that objection as misplaced.
[SAMIN-DURR:70:20-21/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The objection to the adjectival analysis is mistaken: its issue is an adverbial phrase preceding its governor, whereas the real prohibited order would put an adjective’s governed element before the adjective.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p226/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Humans are innately impatient: when harmed they panic, are overwhelmed by fear, and despair of future good.
[BURHAN:v3p36/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The clauses describing the human as anxious when harmed and withholding when prosperous explain هلوعا; explanatory clauses are common in the Qur’an.
[BURHAN:v3p36/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinnī says one should not stop before an explanatory clause, because it completes the explanation much like a relative clause or adjective completes its noun.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p149/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | When even slight harm touches a person, the haluʿ person falls into extreme distress, the opposite of patience.
[DURR-FULL:v8p283/r9] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · علي | reports | A report attributed to Ali says a sick person's groaning is recorded: a patient person earns good deeds, while one who despairs is recorded as haluʿ and receives no reward.
[ITQAN:v3p193#2/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · أهل البيان | reports | The people of rhetoric describe an explanatory clause as something added to remove ambiguity and clarify what came before it.
[ITQAN:v3p193#2/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · أبو العالية وغيره | reports | Abu al-Aliya and others take the clauses about his reaction to harm and good as an explanation of هلوعا.
[ITQAN:v3p193#2/r8] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن جني | holds | Ibn Jinni says one should not pause before an explanatory sentence because it completes and functions as part of what it explains.
[BURSEVI:v10p123/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās’s reported explanation says harm such as poverty or illness makes a person excessively despairing through ignorance of divine decree.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p61#4/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Here الشر refers to poverty, illness, and similar troubles, and its definite article denotes the whole class of harm.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p62/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | جزوعا means repeatedly and intensely panicking; al-Raghib says panic exceeds sadness because it diverts and cuts a person off from what they were doing.

v29p62/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib connects the root to cutting a rope in half, then to a valley's end, multicolored beads or meat, and a date that has ripened halfway.
[ELMALILI:70:8-35/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | When pain, hardship, poverty, or illness touches a person, he complains, writhes, cries out, cannot endure it, and seeks help from others.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p166/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Verses 19–21 interrupt the discussion between the one who hoards and the exception for worshippers; they summarize the human trait that drives greed and retention. | mentions 70:17, 70:22
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p166/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | This is a rebuke, not an excuse or justification for hoarding; fear of losing what benefits them explains the trait but does not absolve it.
[TABATABAI:70:19-21/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | prefers | Haluʿ means intense eagerness; the following verses aptly explain it as panic at harm and withholding when good comes.
[TABATABAI:70:19-21/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Human eagerness targets what a person sees as good or useful for himself, producing distress at harm and selfish withholding of benefits.
[TABATABAI:70:19-21/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Innate eagerness rooted in self-love is not itself a vice; it enables pursuit of happiness and becomes blameworthy only through excess, deficiency, or poor judgment.
[TABATABAI:70:19-21/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Children initially pursue whatever their instincts present as good and resist sharing; reason later revises their judgments, while persistent appetite can lead to rejecting truth and violating others' rights.
[TABATABAI:70:19-35/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | As reason develops, eagerness can turn toward real good: fear of sin and haste toward forgiveness, while worldly hardship and duty call for the patience God prescribes.
[TABATABAI:70:19-35/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | When people ignore reason and follow appetite without limits, they turn a God-given means of happiness into a cause of misery, withdrawal, and hoarding.
[ASAD-NOTES:70:19#n8/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · Jawhari | reports | Jazu combines impatience with lamenting one's misfortune, making it the opposite of sabr.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p463/r8] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | People generally become frustrated and complain when God punishes them even a little for their deeds.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:70:19/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | When struck by poverty, illness, fear, or other hardship, a person may complain, cry out, and lose hope.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p126/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The author observes that the descriptions in al-Muʾminūn and al-Maʿārij are strongly parallel but also differ in wording and order. | mentions 23:1, 23:2, 23:3, 23:4, 23:5, 23:6, 23:7, 23:8, 23:9, 23:10, 23:11
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p155/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | reports | A cited observation contrasts a healthy wealthy person who withholds beneficence with the same person when ill, who panics and begins making bequests.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p155/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr says harm makes a person panic, feel terror, and despair of future good, while a blessing makes him withhold from others and refuse God’s due from it.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p155/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · فتح القدير | reports | Fatḥ al-Qadīr, citing al-Ṣiḥāḥ, glosses halūʿ as extreme greed and the worst, most excessive panic; calamity yields much panic and prosperity yields much withholding.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p155/r4] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Jazaʿ is the opposite of patience, as shown by the Qurʾānic pairing of whether people panic or remain patient in 14:21. | mentions 14:21
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p155/r5] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The passage puts harm before good because the sūra opens with a demand for punishment and has just depicted the criminal’s wish to ransom himself and the blaze that tears at the skin. | mentions 70:1, 70:11, 70:15, 70:16
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p156/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Beginning with harm is appropriate to the sūra’s opening demand for punishment and its atmosphere; panic also contrasts with the command to the Prophet to be patient with beautiful patience. | mentions 70:1, 70:5
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p158/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Persistent prayer treats panic by cultivating continuous patience; people often pray but fail to maintain attention because their thoughts and distractions take much of the prayer away.
[STUDYQURAN:70:19/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The passage echoes 41:49–51, where people persist in asking for good, despair when harmed, and withdraw after receiving mercy. | mentions 41:49, 41:50, 41:51
[STUDYQURAN:70:19/r10] STUDYQURAN · R | reports | Those who possess the eight qualities in 70:22–35 are exempt from the blameworthy state described here. | mentions 70:22, 70:23, 70:24, 70:25, 70:26, 70:27, 70:28, 70:29, 70:30, 70:31, 70:32, 70:33, 70:34, 70:35
[STUDYQURAN:70:19/r6] STUDYQURAN · R | reports | Evil and good may mean misfortune and good fortune generally, or specifically illness and poverty versus health and wealth.
[STUDYQURAN:70:19/r7] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Jazūʿ conveys distress at misfortune and lack of forbearance, the opposite of the patience enjoined in 70:5. | mentions 70:5
[STUDYQURAN:70:19/r8] STUDYQURAN · al-Rāzī | reports | To overcome anxiety, recognize that circumstances come from God and be content with them.
[STUDYQURAN:70:19/r9] STUDYQURAN · R | reports | Al-Rāzī says health and wealth should be spent to seek gain in the Hereafter rather than this life.
